cues.x: The 4-Hour Workweek, by Timothy Ferriss.
Let me start you in an office in San Jose, California, in the year 2004, with a twenty-seven year old man who has built exactly the business he said he wanted and is quietly falling apart inside it.
His name is Tim Ferriss.

A few years earlier he had graduated from Princeton, taken a job in sales at a data storage company, hated it, and started a small business out of his apartment selling a sports nutrition supplement called BrainQUICKEN.
It worked.
Orders came in.
Revenue climbed to something like forty thousand dollars a month.
By every measure his friends could see, he had made it.
He was his own boss.
He owned the thing.
And he was working fourteen hour days, seven days a week.
He was answering every customer email personally.
He was approving every refund personally.
He was checking inventory personally.
He had built himself a company that could not run for a single afternoon without him standing inside it holding the walls up.
He describes waking up in the middle of the night with his jaw clenched, checking email at three in the morning because a single unanswered message felt like a fire.
At one point he considered simply shutting the whole thing down, because ending it seemed easier than continuing it.
Instead he did something slightly ridiculous.
He decided to leave.
Not to sell the business, not to quit it, just to physically remove himself from it and go to Europe for what he told everyone was a short sabbatical.
He was terrified.
He was convinced that in his absence the whole thing would collapse, the customers would riot, the suppliers would fail, and he would come home to rubble.
He had bought a plane ticket he could not really justify, and then he spent weeks not getting on the plane.
He kept finding reasons.
And in that stalling, he did an exercise that ended up being the intellectual heart of the whole book, an exercise borrowed straight from the Stoics.
He sat down and wrote out, in obsessive detail, what the actual worst case scenario was.
Not the vague dread.
The specifics.
The worst case, when he wrote it down, was this: the business would decline, he would lose most of the income, he would have to come home, move somewhere cheap, get a job, and rebuild.
That was it.
That was the monster.
And when he looked at it written on paper, he noticed something that changes everything: it was a temporary, recoverable, entirely survivable outcome.
He had been paralysed by something that, spelled out in plain language, was a bad six months.
So he got on the plane.
He went to London, and then he kept going.
And here is the part that turned into a book.
Away from the office, forced to work in short bursts on hotel internet, he could not do fourteen hours a day.
He had maybe an hour.
So he had to work out what actually mattered.
And when he did that, when he stripped the business down to only the things that genuinely produced results, the business did not collapse.
It got better.
Revenue went up.
His working hours went down to something like four a week.
He stayed away for over a year.
He learned to tango in Buenos Aires, well enough to compete.
He trained and swam and read and lived in a way he had told himself he would get to at sixty five.
That is the book.
Not a scheme for laziness.

A very specific argument that most of the work most people do is decorative, that the way we have arranged a working life is close to insane, and that a small number of people have quietly opted out of that arrangement without waiting for permission.
Let me give you the argument properly, because it is more rigorous than the title suggests.
Ferriss calls the target group the New Rich.
And his first move is to attack what he calls the deferred life plan.

That plan goes like this: you work hard for forty years at something you tolerate, you accumulate money, and then at some point near the end you stop and finally do the things you actually wanted to do.
Retirement, in this arrangement, is the reward.
His objection is not moral, it is arithmetic.
He points out three problems with retirement as a goal.
First, it assumes you dislike what you are doing enough to want to escape it for the rest of your life, which is a strange thing to design forty years around.
Second, most people's retirement income, after inflation eats it, buys a fairly modest life, so the reward at the end is smaller than the sacrifice suggested.
And third, and this is the one that lands, if you are ambitious enough to save enough money to retire well, you are usually ambitious enough that sitting still will drive you slowly insane.
The people who most successfully build up to retirement are exactly the people least suited to it.
So Ferriss reframes retirement.
He does not say do not save.
He says retirement should be treated as worst case scenario insurance, a floor under you if your body or your circumstances fail, not the destination.
The destination should be a life you are actually living now, in instalments, all the way through.
And then he introduces the two ideas that make the rest of the book work.
The first is relative income.
Most people compare salaries in absolute terms.
This person earns eighty thousand a year, this one earns a hundred and fifty thousand, so the second is doing better.
Ferriss says that comparison is missing the denominator.
Relative income counts money per hour, and more importantly, money per hour of your life spent, including commuting, including the Sunday night dread, including the phone in the evening.

A person earning fifty thousand who works twenty flexible hours a week from wherever they like has a very different life from someone earning a hundred and fifty thousand for eighty rigid hours in a place they must physically be.
On paper the second is three times richer.
In lived reality the first is often ahead.
The second idea is that the actual currency of the New Rich is not cash.
It is two things: time, meaning control over what you do with your hours, and mobility, meaning control over where you are when you do it.
Money is only a means of buying those two.
Which means, and this is the pivot of the book, you can often get most of the way to a rich life by attacking time and mobility directly, without first getting rich in the traditional sense.
Ferriss then lays out a set of what he calls the rules that change the rules.
Let me give you the best of them, because they run through everything after.
One.
Doing less is not laziness.
He is blunt about this.
Doing less meaningless work so you can concentrate on things of greater importance is not laziness, and being busy is most often a form of laziness, lazy thinking and indiscriminate action.
Sitting in a chair for nine hours is easy.
Deciding what genuinely matters and doing only that is hard, because it requires judgement and it exposes you.
Two.
The timing is never right.
There is never a perfect moment to start a business, have a child, leave a job, or move abroad.
If you wait for all the lights to turn green you will not leave the driveway.
Do it and correct course later.
Three.
Ask forgiveness, not permission.
Most things people fear asking for are not actually catastrophic if done and later explained.
If the damage is small and reversible, act, then explain.
Four.
Emphasise strengths, do not fix weaknesses.
It is far more profitable to multiply results in the two or three things you are genuinely excellent at than to grind an incompetence up to mediocre.
Five.
Things in excess become their opposite.
Too much choice becomes paralysis.
Too much freedom becomes drift.
Too much money past a point stops buying anything.
Six.
Money alone is not the solution.
He is honest that people who become wealthy without having thought about what they want simply become wealthy people who do not know what they want.
And seven, the one that reframes stress.
He splits stress into two kinds.
Distress is the harmful sort: criticism that makes you smaller, deadlines that produce nothing but fear, work that erodes you.
Eustress is the useful sort: the discomfort of a hard training session, a role slightly beyond you, a language you cannot yet speak.
The goal is not a stress free life.
That is a life of no growth.
The goal is to eliminate distress ruthlessly and go looking for eustress on purpose.
Now the structure.
The whole book is built on a four step acronym: D E A L. Definition, Elimination, Automation, Liberation.
If you are an employee you run it in the order D, E, L, A.
If you are self employed or building something, you run it D, E, A, L.
Let me take each one properly.
Definition first.
This is where you replace the vague ambition of "be successful" with something that can actually be aimed at.
The most valuable single exercise in the book lives here, and it is called fear setting.
Ferriss argues that what stops people is almost never a rational assessment of a downside.
It is unexamined dread, an undefined cloud, and clouds cannot be argued with.
So you define it.
You take a sheet of paper and three columns.
In the first column you write down, in painful and specific detail, the absolute worst that could happen if you did the thing you are avoiding.
Not "it would be bad".
Actual sentences.
I would lose this much money.
I would have to tell these people.
I would have to move here.
Then you score each one for how permanently damaging it really is, on a scale of one to ten.
Most of them come out at a three or a four, and are temporary.
Second column: for each of those worst cases, what could you do to repair the damage, or to get back to where you are now?
Almost always the answer is embarrassingly ordinary.
Get another job.
Move back.
Borrow from a friend for a few months.
Sell the car.
The repair is nearly always available.
Third column, and this is where it stops being an intellectual exercise: what are the costs, financially, emotionally, and physically, of inaction?
Of not doing it.
Not just for six months, but for one year, and for three years, and for five.
Because we are extremely good at pricing the risk of action and almost completely blind to the compounding cost of staying still.
Five more years in a job that is quietly draining you is not a neutral outcome.
It is a very large cost that simply does not send you an invoice.
Ferriss's line here is the one people remember: what we fear doing most is usually what we most need to do.
And the practical version: name your fears in detail and they stop being fears.
They become a to do list with a risk attached.

Sitting alongside fear setting are what Ferriss calls comfort challenges, and they are odd little exercises scattered through the book that turn out to be the mechanism by which the whole philosophy actually gets installed in a person.
He argues that the limiting factor for most people is not capability, it is a low tolerance for social discomfort.
So he asks you to practise being uncomfortable in tiny, harmless ways.
Hold eye contact with strangers until they look away first.
Ask ten strangers in a day for their phone number and get rejected on purpose, so that rejection stops being a catastrophe and becomes a data point.
Lie down on the floor of a busy public place for ten seconds, say nothing, get up, and walk on.
Ask for a discount at a coffee shop where nobody asks for discounts.
Ferriss is not being playful for its own sake.
He is training the exact muscle you will need when you ask your boss for a remote trial, or email a stranger who could change your career, or tell a customer you no longer want their business.
The people who cannot do those things are almost never blocked by logic.
They are blocked by a two second flinch, and the flinch is trainable.
His own life is the demonstration.

He went to Buenos Aires as a tourist, decided to learn tango, and within about six months was competing at a level that put him among the top performers at a world championship and into the Guinness records for a specific tango move.

Years earlier, with almost no formal background, he had entered and won a Chinese kickboxing championship by studying the rulebook harder than his opponents did and exploiting what it actually said rather than what everyone assumed it said.
You can find that admirable or you can find it a bit sharp, and I will come back to that honestly later.

But the pattern underneath both stories is consistent, and it is the same pattern as fear setting: he examines the thing everyone treats as fixed, and discovers it was never fixed, it was just unquestioned.
Then comes dreamlining, which is his replacement for goal setting.
He argues that "what do you want" is a useless question because it is too big and too abstract.
People answer "to be happy", which cannot be acted on.
So he changes the question to: what would you do, if there were no way you could fail?
And then he forces two things on the answer that make it real.
First, a timeline.
Two of them: a six month timeline and a twelve month timeline.
Second, and this is the clever part, everything gets converted into money.
You write out five things you want to have, five things you want to be, and five things you want to do, in each timeline.
Then you take the "be" items and convert them into "do" items, because being cannot be scheduled and doing can.
If you want to be a great cook, the doing is: cook this specific dish for these four friends by this date.
If you want to be fluent in Spanish, the doing is: hold a fifteen minute conversation with a native speaker by this date.
Being is a fog.
Doing has an edge.
Then you cost it.
For each dream, you write the actual price.
Not the imagined price, the researched price.
And then you do the arithmetic that makes the whole thing land.

You take the one time costs, spread them over the months, add the monthly running costs, add your existing monthly living expenses, multiply by about one point three to give yourself a buffer, and you get what he calls Target Monthly Income.
Divide by thirty and you have Target Daily Income.
The reason this exercise is worth doing is what happens next.
Almost everybody who does it honestly discovers that the number is far, far smaller than the number in their head.
People carry around a belief that the life they want requires being rich.
Here is what happened when he ran it on his own business.
He had something like a hundred and twenty wholesale customers.
When he actually looked, five of them produced about ninety five percent of his revenue.
Five.
Everyone else was noise.

And when he ran the second question, the problem question, he found that a small handful of customers, mostly small ones, generated the overwhelming majority of the complaints, the chased payments, the emails, the anxiety.
So he did something that felt insane at the time.
He stopped actively servicing the bottom of the list, moved them to a passive, order it if you want it arrangement, and in some cases fired the worst of them outright.
Then he took the five that mattered and gave them concentrated attention, called them, asked what they needed, made it easier for them to order more.
His hours dropped from something like eighty a week to fifteen, and his income roughly doubled inside a couple of months.
Now, the honest caveat: not every job lets you fire your customers.
But the underlying move is available to everyone.
Take your customers, your clients, your projects, your tasks, your commitments, even your social calendar, and sort them by results produced and by misery produced.
The lists will be shockingly lopsided.
Then act on both ends.
The second law is Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
Give a task a week and it takes a week and feels important the whole time.
Give the same task two hours with a hard stop and it usually gets done in two hours, at roughly the same quality, because the short deadline forces you to do only the essential parts.
Ferriss's insight is to use these two laws together, because either one alone fails.
Use eighty twenty alone and you identify the important things, then let them sprawl.
Use short deadlines alone and you become very fast at unimportant work.
Combined, they give you the actual instruction: identify the few tasks that contribute most, then schedule them with absurdly short, clear deadlines.
He offers a daily filter for this that I find genuinely useful.
Ask, at the start of the day, "if this is the only thing I accomplish today, will I be satisfied with my day?"
Pick one, maybe two things that pass.
Do them before anything else.
And when you find yourself unsure whether to do something, ask, "am I being productive, or just active?
Am I inventing things to do to avoid the important?"
Because busywork is the most socially acceptable form of avoidance ever invented.
Then comes the low information diet, and this is the part of the book that has aged into being more relevant rather than less.
Ferriss argues that most information consumption is not preparation, it is procrastination in a respectable costume.
His prescription is deliberately extreme: a one week media fast.
No news, no television, no news websites, no unnecessary reading, no browsing.
If something genuinely important happens in the world, someone will tell you, and he suggests actively asking someone at lunch, "anything important happening in the world?"
Underneath the extreme version is a principle worth keeping: switch from just in case learning to just in time learning.
Do not read about a country for months in case you go.
Go, and learn what you need in the week before.
Do not consume material that you will not act on within a short window.
The test is: will I definitely use this information for something immediate and important?
Then interruptions, which he taxonomises in a way that makes them fixable.
Time wasters are things that can simply be ignored with little or no consequence.
Most email, most meetings, most phone calls, most of the internet.
The fix is batching and cutting off access.

He is famous for this one: check email twice a day, at a fixed time, say noon and four in the afternoon, and never first thing in the morning, because starting your day inside other people's requests hands the day away before you have used it.
Put an autoresponder on that tells people honestly that you check twice daily and gives them a phone number for genuine emergencies.
Almost nobody uses the number.
The same batching logic applies to everything with a setup cost.

Laundry, errands, invoicing, admin. Doing something once a week costs enormously less total time than doing it in twelve interruptions across the week, because every interruption charges you twice: once for the task and once for the reload of your attention afterwards.
Time consumers are the repetitive tasks and requests that must be dealt with but can be batched or streamlined.
And then the third category, the important one, empowerment failures.
These are the moments when someone has to come to you for approval because they do not have the authority to act.
Every one of them is an interruption you personally installed.
Ferriss's solution here is one of the most practical things in the book and it applies to any manager listening.
He gave his customer service outsourcers and staff a rule: you can make any decision that costs less than a hundred dollars without asking me.
Just do it, and keep a note of what you decided.
Then he reviewed the notes monthly and moved the ceiling up when the decisions were good.

The result was that the flood of "can I refund this customer, can I reship this order" emails simply stopped, and, this is the part people find surprising, the customers were happier, because they got instant answers rather than waiting for one busy man to wake up.
The general principle: every rule you make that requires someone to check with you is a permanent tax on your own attention.
Replace approval with a policy and a budget.

He also recommends the not to do list, which sits next to your to do list and is often more valuable: do not answer calls from unknown numbers, do not check email first thing or last thing, do not agree to meetings without a clear agenda and end time, do not let people ramble, do not carry a phone into the evening.
And on meetings, he has a rule I have watched people apply with immediate effect: never attend a meeting whose purpose is not clearly defined, and always ask for an agenda and an end time in advance.
Most meetings that cannot survive that question were never necessary.
Now Automation, which is where the book gets both its most famous and its most misunderstood material.
The first half is outsourcing.

Ferriss was, in 2007, one of the first mainstream writers to point out that you could hire a remote assistant in India or the Philippines for a few dollars an hour to handle scheduling, research, data entry, customer email, bookings, and chasing.
He gives real examples, including his own experiments with firms like Brickwork in Bangalore, and various readers who tried it.
The stories are funny and instructive.

One reader famously outsourced an apology to his wife, having his assistant send the flowers and the message after an argument, which Ferriss includes partly as comedy and partly as a warning about the boundary between delegating tasks and delegating your life.
Another reader had two assistants on opposite sides of the world so work continued around the clock.
Others discovered that vague instructions produce vague, expensive results.
But the crucial lesson in the outsourcing chapter is not "hire cheap labour".
It is this: never automate something that can be eliminated, and never delegate something that can be automated.
That sequence matters enormously.
If you skip Elimination and jump straight to Automation, you simply pay someone else to do work that should not exist, and now you have both the cost and the management overhead.
Ferriss says it plainly: the goal is not to have a busy assistant.
It is to notice, when you try to write down instructions for a task, that quite a lot of your tasks cannot survive being written down, because when you look at them clearly they are pointless.
Delegation also teaches you to define things precisely, which is a genuine skill.
If you cannot explain a task in one clear paragraph, you probably do not understand it.
The second half of Automation is the muse.
This is the part everyone remembers, and the part most people get wrong.
A muse, in Ferriss's language, is a small, automated business whose only job is to fund your target monthly income without consuming your life.
It is explicitly not a startup you want to grow into an empire.
Different goal.
He is not against building a large company, he is saying that if what you actually want is time and mobility, then a business designed to be sold or scaled will give you the opposite for years.
So he gives criteria for what to build, and they are all designed around one thing: removing yourself from the process.
Price it between roughly fifty and two hundred dollars.
Cheaper than fifty and you need enormous volume, which means enormous customer service.
More expensive and you need consultative selling, which means you personally on the phone.
It should be something you can produce or source within three or four weeks, so you do not spend a year building before you learn anything.
The frequently asked questions about it should fit on one page or less.
If a customer needs a long conversation to understand it, you cannot remove yourself.
It should be fully outsourceable to manufacture and fulfil.
And it should serve a market of specialists, a defined group you already understand or belong to, that you can reach through their existing magazines, forums, associations and communities.
Ferriss is very insistent here: pick a market first, then find a product for it.
Most people do the reverse, invent a product, and then discover they have no way to reach anybody.
Now, the method that made this chapter famous: test the product before you make it.
The traditional path is to invest money in inventory, then discover whether anyone wants it.
Ferriss inverts it.
You build a small landing page describing the product exactly as if it exists, with the price, the benefits, the details.
You add a buy button.
You drive a small amount of paid traffic at it for a few days, at a modest daily budget, targeting the search terms your specialist market would actually type.
Then you count.
Not how many people visit.
How many people click the buy button, which is the only honest measure of intent, because clicking that button is the moment of decision.
And when they click, they land on a page that says, honestly, that the product is temporarily out of stock, apologises, and offers to notify them when it is available.
No money is taken.
Nobody is charged.
You have bought, for a small advertising budget, a real answer to the only question that matters: will strangers actually buy this?
The result is that you can kill five bad ideas in three weeks for the price of a nice dinner, instead of killing one bad idea in a year for the price of a car.
And when a test does show real demand, you build it knowing there are buyers.
Ferriss then adds the architecture that keeps the muse from becoming a job.
Once orders exist, you route them straight to an outsourced fulfilment company.
You route customer service to an outsourced service company.
You give both of them decision rules and spending limits so they never need you.
You remove your own email address from the loop.
He describes this as removing yourself from the flow of information, and it is the moment where the business stops being self employment and becomes an income stream.

He is also honest about the failure modes: the temptation to keep tinkering, the temptation to say yes to every opportunity for growth, the customers who eat your margin, and the fact that a business without a leader still needs a very well designed set of rules.
And then Liberation, the fourth step, and the one aimed squarely at people who have a job and no intention of starting a business.

Ferriss's argument is that the office is largely a legacy of a time when work required physical proximity to equipment and paper, and that for a large number of jobs, the requirement to be in a specific chair in a specific building is now a convention rather than a necessity.
His method for escaping it is not to ask for permission in one big conversation, because a big request invites a big no.
It is a staged, evidence based campaign.
Step one, make yourself more valuable, not less.
Increase your output visibly, so that losing you becomes expensive and accommodating you becomes cheap.
Step two, prove the concept with an accident.
Work remotely for a day for a legitimate reason, being ill, waiting for a delivery, a plumber, whatever.
Then, and this is the essential bit, do a lot of high visibility work that day and make sure the results are seen.
Send the report, close the thing, produce the number.
Step three, quantify.
Track your output at home versus in the office.
Ferriss's claim, borne out by a lot of research since, is that most knowledge workers produce more away from the interruption machine of an open office.
You need this as data, not as opinion, because your manager's fear is not that you dislike the office, it is that you will do less work.
Step four, propose a small, reversible trial.
Not "I would like to work remotely".
Instead: "I would like to trial working from home on Tuesdays and Thursdays for two weeks, and if productivity does not improve on the measures we agree, we go straight back."
A small, reversible, measured request with a built in exit is very hard to refuse, and it puts your manager in the position of running an experiment rather than making a concession.
Step five, extend gradually.
Two days becomes four.
Four becomes full time.

Full time becomes location independent, at which point nobody actually knows or cares whether you are in the next suburb or another continent, as long as the work lands and you are reachable at agreed times.
And if the answer is no at every stage, that itself is information about whether the job is compatible with the life you have defined.
Once you are free of the location, Ferriss makes the argument for what he calls mini retirements, and this is his replacement for the deferred life plan.

Instead of saving up a huge block of freedom for the end, you take it in chunks throughout: one to six months somewhere else, living rather than touring, repeated every year or two across your working life.
The economics are counterintuitive and worth stating clearly.
In many parts of the world, living well costs dramatically less than living averagely in an expensive city.
If your income is earned in a strong currency and your costs are paid in a weaker one, the arithmetic of your life changes completely.
This is geoarbitrage.
It is the same reason Ferriss could live in Buenos Aires and Berlin on money that would have been unremarkable in California.
And he is careful to distinguish a mini retirement from a holiday.
A holiday is a frantic two week attempt to see everything, which is exhausting and produces almost no change in you.
A mini retirement is slow.
You rent a flat rather than a hotel.
You learn some of the language.
You have a routine.
You get bored, and then you get past bored, which is where the interesting part begins.
The point is not to see places.
It is to interrupt the momentum of your ordinary life long enough to notice what you actually want.
Which brings me to the most honest chapter in the book, and the one people who dismiss it have usually not read: filling the void.
Ferriss admits that when he finally got what he wanted, the freedom and the money and the empty calendar, he was miserable.
He describes it plainly.
Removing the thing that was consuming him did not automatically produce joy.
It produced a large silence, and in the silence came a set of uncomfortable questions about identity and worth that his eighty hour weeks had been very effectively drowning out.
Work, he realised, had been doing a lot of psychological labour beyond producing income.
It had been telling him who he was.
His conclusion is that freedom is a container, not a contents.
You have to fill it deliberately, and he suggests two things that reliably do the job.
The first is learning, especially learning that is difficult and measurable: a language, a sport, an instrument, a physical skill.
The second is service, contributing to something outside yourself, though he insists you find your own version rather than adopting somebody else's cause out of duty.
He also names the two questions that torment newly free people.
"Who am I, if I am not my job?"
And "what am I doing with my life?"
His answer to the second is to make it smaller and answerable: not "what is my life's purpose", but "what excites me right now, and what can I get better at?"
Excitement, he argues, is a more useful compass than happiness, because happiness is too vague a target to steer by.

Ferriss closes the practical part of the book with a list of the mistakes he watches newly free people make, and they are worth hearing because they are the ways the whole thing quietly reverses itself.
Losing sight of dreams and drifting back into work for its own sake.
This is the most common one.
The business gets automated, the time appears, and within four months the person has filled every hour of it with more business, because that is the only script they know.
Micromanaging and emailing to fill time.
When you have removed yourself from the flow of information, there is a powerful urge to reinsert yourself, to check, to improve, to reply to something you had successfully arranged never to see.
Resist it, or you will rebuild the cage by hand.
Handling problems your outsourcers or colleagues can handle.
Every time you take back a decision you had delegated, you teach everyone that the delegation was not real.
Chasing customers, particularly unqualified or international ones, when you already have enough.
Growth for its own sake is how a muse turns back into a job.
Answering email that will not result in a sale or that can be answered by a policy or an autoresponder.
Working where you live, sleep or should relax.
He is firm on this: separate the places, or the work bleeds into everything.

Not performing a thorough eighty twenty analysis every two to four weeks, because the distribution shifts, and the twenty percent that mattered last quarter is not automatically the twenty percent that matters now.
Striving for perfection rather than great, or simply good enough.
Perfectionism, in his framing, is procrastination with a respectable name.
Blowing small problems out of proportion as an excuse to work.
This one is subtle and true.
A person who is uncomfortable with free time will find a crisis, because a crisis is permission to be busy again.
And the last one, which is the emotional core of the closing chapters: making non time sensitive issues urgent in order to justify work.
If nothing is on fire, and you cannot bear that, you will light something.
Now let me be a fair guide and tell you honestly what has aged in this book, because it was written in 2007 and some of it shows.
The tactical detail is dated.
Some of the specific services he names no longer exist or have changed.
The advertising costs he quotes for testing an idea are a fraction of what they now cost.
The outsourcing landscape is completely different, and quite a lot of what he paid an assistant to do in 2007 is now done by software in seconds.
The information product market he describes as wide open has become extremely crowded.
There is also a fair criticism of the ethics in places.

The book contains a certain amount of gaming: the story of him winning a national kickboxing title by exploiting the weigh in rules and a technicality about pushing opponents off the platform, the general appetite for finding the loophole.
Some readers find that admirable and some find it grubby, and both readings are reasonable.
Ferriss is straightforwardly telling you he looks for the rules that are actually enforced rather than the rules people assume, which is a real skill and also, in some hands, an unpleasant one.
And the title oversells.
Very few people run a business on four hours a week for long.
Ferriss himself did not, for long.
What he actually built was a business that could survive without him, which is a different and better claim.
But strip out the dated tactics and what remains is a set of ideas that have held up remarkably well, and in some cases predicted the world we now live in.
Remote work as default.
Output measured rather than hours measured.
The idea that attention is the scarce resource and that most information consumption is a cost, not an investment.
The notion that you should design your life around time and mobility rather than around income alone.
All of that reads now as ordinary.
It did not in 2007.
So let me leave you with the practical part, the things you could actually do this week.
First, do the fear setting exercise on the one thing you have been avoiding.
Three columns.
Define the worst case in detail, write down how you would repair it, and then honestly price the cost of doing nothing for one, three and five years.
Do it on paper.
The paper is the whole trick, because a fear you can read is a fear you can argue with.
Second, do the dreamlining arithmetic.
Pick a six month timeline.
Write five things you want to have, five you want to be, five you want to do.
Convert the being into doing with a date and a measurable outcome.
Then cost the whole thing and work out your real target monthly income.
Most people find the number is a fraction of what they assumed, and that alone changes what feels possible.
Third, run the eighty twenty audit in both directions.
List your clients, projects, tasks and commitments.
Which fifth of them produces most of your results?
Which fifth produces most of your stress?
Then do something about both ends this week, not next quarter.
Even one call to your best client, and one honest ending of your worst commitment, will change your month.
Fourth, batch your email and put a hard stop on your day.
Two fixed checks, never first thing.
Set an autoresponder that tells people when you check and how to reach you if it is genuinely urgent.
Expect it to feel unbearable for three days and normal by the second week.
Fifth, find your empowerment failures.
Look for every situation where someone has to ask your permission to do something small.
Replace each one with a written rule and a spending limit.
You will get a quieter inbox and, usually, faster and happier customers.
Sixth, if you have an idea for a product or a service, do not build it.
Test it.
Put up a single page describing it honestly as though it exists, at a real price, with a real button.
Send a small amount of traffic at it.
Count the clicks on the button.
Tell the people who click, truthfully, that it is not available yet and ask if they want to be told when it is.
You will learn in five days what most people take a year and a great deal of money to learn.
And seventh, if you are employed and want more freedom, do not ask for it.
Earn it, evidence it, and then propose a small reversible trial with measurable outcomes and a built in way to go back.
Two days a week for two weeks is an experiment.
Permanent remote work is a concession.
People say yes to experiments.
The deepest idea in this book is not about working four hours.

It is about noticing that a great deal of what we do is unexamined convention that we have mistaken for necessity: the hours, the location, the sequence of a life, the belief that freedom comes at the end.
Ferriss's real contribution is the habit of asking, of every constraint you are living inside, a simple and slightly rude question.
Says who?
And then, having written down exactly what happens if the answer turns out to be nobody, getting on the plane.
